A square's diagonals decrease at the rate of  $2\text{ m}\text{/min}.$ At what rate is the area of the square decreasing when the diagonals are $3\text{ m}$ long each?
question.worked_solution:
Let $h$ and $A$ be the length of the diagonals and the area of the square, respectively. Using the Pythagorean theorem, it can be shown that the relationship between $A$ and $h$ is

$$
A=\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}.
$$

We want to find

$$
\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}h}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot h.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that $h$ decreases at a rate of $2\,\text{m/min},$ so

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we want to compute the rate of change of the area when the diagonal has length $h=3.$ Substituting this information into our expression for $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =-2\cdot 3=-6{\text{ m}}^{2}\text{/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the area of the square is decreasing at a rate of $6{\text{ m}}^{2}\text{/min}.$
